definition_text: When we say AI, we mean the systems in use today: chatbots and assistants, image and voice tools, recommendation systems, and software that makes or supports decisions about people. A few questions ask about more capable future AI; those say so. There are no right answers. If you are unsure, pick the answer closest to how you lean; at the end of each section we will ask how settled your views are.

items.stem: Over the next ten years, AI will make important medical and scientific discoveries happen sooner.
items.short: AI will speed up important medical and scientific discoveries

items.stem: AI will give ordinary people access to expert help, such as legal, medical or financial advice, that they cannot afford today.
items.short: AI will give ordinary people affordable access to expert help

items.stem: In my own life, AI tools are likely to save me real time or money.
items.short: AI tools will save you real time or money

items.stem: Over the next ten years, AI will raise living standards for most people in my country.
items.short: AI will raise living standards for most people in your country

items.stem: Most of what is promised about AI's benefits will never actually arrive.
items.short: most of AI's promised benefits will never arrive

items.stem: AI mostly makes existing products a little more convenient; it will not change much that matters.
items.short: AI will mostly make products a little more convenient, not change much that matters

items.stem: For most people, AI will make daily life harder rather than easier.
items.short: AI will make daily life harder for most people

items.stem: I expect AI to disappoint in the areas where it is supposed to help most, such as health and education.
items.short: AI will disappoint where it is supposed to help most, such as health and education

items.stem: AI will eliminate more jobs than it creates in my country over the next ten years.
items.short: AI will eliminate more jobs than it creates

items.stem: AI will make it harder to know what is true, because fake text, images and video will be everywhere.
items.short: AI will make it harder to know what is true

items.stem: AI will widen the gap between rich and poor even if the economy as a whole grows.
items.short: AI will widen the gap between rich and poor

items.stem: Some harms from AI will be impossible to undo once they have happened.
items.short: some harms from AI will be impossible to undo

items.stem: Worries about AI are mostly exaggerated by the media.
items.short: worries about AI are mostly exaggerated by the media

items.stem: Society will adapt to AI the way it adapted to the internet, without lasting damage.
items.short: society will adapt to AI without lasting damage

items.stem: The risks of AI can be handled with ordinary laws and common sense.
items.short: AI's risks can be handled with ordinary laws and common sense

items.stem: Fears that AI will escape human control belong in science fiction, not public policy.
items.short: fears of AI escaping human control belong in science fiction

items.stem: It is better to slow down AI development and get the rules right, even if useful tools arrive years later.
items.short: it's better to slow AI down and get the rules right, even if useful tools arrive later

items.stem: When a new AI capability is powerful but hard to evaluate, it should be released in stages rather than all at once.
items.short: powerful but hard-to-evaluate AI should be released in stages

items.stem: If experts cannot agree whether a new AI system is safe, it should not be released until they can.
items.short: AI shouldn't be released while experts disagree about whether it is safe

items.stem: Governments should be able to pause the development of the most powerful AI systems while risks are unclear.
items.short: governments should be able to pause the most powerful AI while risks are unclear

items.stem: Delaying AI also causes harm, by postponing cures and discoveries that could help people now.
items.short: delaying AI has real costs, because it postpones useful discoveries

items.stem: Companies should be free to release new AI tools and fix problems as they appear, rather than wait for approval.
items.short: companies should be free to release AI tools and fix problems as they appear

items.stem: The best way to find out whether an AI tool is safe is to let people use it.
items.short: the best way to learn whether AI is safe is to let people use it

items.stem: Countries that slow down AI will be left behind by those that do not.
items.short: countries that slow down on AI will be left behind

items.stem: Which is closer to your view?
options: Keep safety rules for AI even if development is slower.
Develop AI as fast as possible even if some rules are loosened.
items.short: safety rules should stay even if AI development is slower

items.stem: Before an AI system is used for important decisions about people, it should be tested by an independent body that does not work for the company.
items.short: AI used for important decisions about people should be tested by an independent body first

items.stem: Governments should set binding rules for AI rather than leave it to industry codes of conduct.
items.short: governments should set binding rules for AI

items.stem: Even well-run AI companies need an outside regulator checking their work.
items.short: even well-run AI companies need an outside regulator

items.stem: AI companies should be legally responsible when their systems cause harm.
items.short: AI companies should be legally responsible for harms their systems cause

items.stem: The people who build AI understand it best, so they should be the ones setting the rules for it.
items.short: the people who build AI should set the rules for it

items.stem: Strict government rules on AI will mostly protect big companies that can afford lawyers and hurt smaller ones.
items.short: strict AI rules mostly protect big companies

items.stem: Rules written by regulators today will be out of date before they take effect.
items.short: AI rules will be out of date before they take effect
items.source: Petry Substack lesson; Stewards vs Precautionists split

items.stem: Competition between AI companies will do more to keep AI safe than government rules will.
items.short: competition will do more to keep AI safe than government rules

items.stem: Which is closer to your view?
options: Rules for AI should be written by government and enforced by law.
Rules for AI should be agreed and enforced by the companies themselves.
items.short: rules for AI should be written by government and enforced by law

items.stem: International agreements on the most capable AI systems are worth pursuing even if rival countries benefit from them too.
items.short: international agreements on the most capable AI are worth pursuing even if rivals benefit

items.stem: My country should develop AI together with allies rather than on its own.
items.short: your country should develop AI together with allies

items.stem: My country should build its own AI capability rather than depend on foreign companies or governments.
items.short: your country should build its own AI capability

items.stem: Having more advanced AI than other countries matters more than having international rules.
items.short: being ahead in AI matters more than international rules

items.stem: When AI influences an important decision about a person, such as a loan, a job or a medical treatment, that person should be able to appeal to a human.
items.short: people should be able to appeal AI-influenced decisions to a human

items.stem: Some decisions should always be made by a human, even if an AI would make them more accurately.
items.short: some decisions should always be made by a human, even at some cost in accuracy

items.stem: I would rather have a human explain a decision I disagree with than an AI that gets it right more often.
items.short: a human who can explain a decision is better than a more accurate AI

items.stem: A decision that could change someone's life should not be left to an AI, even with a human checking afterwards.
items.short: life-changing decisions shouldn't be left to AI, even with a human checking

items.stem: If evidence showed an AI made fairer decisions than human judges or managers, I would support letting it decide.
items.short: AI should decide if evidence shows it's fairer than people

items.stem: Insisting on a human in every decision will mean slower, more expensive and more biased outcomes.
items.short: insisting on a human in every decision makes outcomes worse

items.stem: For everyday choices with little at stake, I am happy to let AI decide for me without checking.
items.short: AI can make low-stakes everyday choices without being checked

items.stem: In many situations, a human reviewing an AI's decision adds cost without adding safety.
items.short: human review of AI decisions often adds cost without adding safety

items.stem: For a decision about you, which would you choose?
options: A human decision-maker who is less accurate but can explain the decision.
An AI system that is more accurate but cannot explain its decisions.
items.short: a human who can explain a decision is preferable to a more accurate AI that cannot

items.stem: Companies that replace workers with AI should pay toward retraining or supporting those workers.
items.short: companies that replace workers with AI should help support them

items.stem: If AI makes the economy much more productive, governments should make sure the gains reach people whose work was replaced.
items.short: governments should make sure AI's gains reach people whose work was replaced

items.stem: Workers should have a say before AI is introduced into their workplace.
items.short: workers should have a say before AI comes into their workplace

items.stem: Public money spent on AI research should come with conditions that the results benefit the public, not only investors.
items.short: publicly funded AI research should benefit the public, not only investors

items.stem: The best way to spread the benefits of AI is to let new companies and services compete.
items.short: competition is the best way to spread AI's benefits

items.stem: Businesses have no special obligation to workers replaced by AI beyond what the law already requires.
items.short: businesses owe nothing extra to workers replaced by AI

items.stem: Trying to share AI's gains through taxes or rules would slow the economy and leave everyone worse off.
items.short: sharing AI's gains through taxes or rules would leave everyone worse off

items.stem: People whose jobs change because of AI should adapt, as workers have with every past technology.
items.short: people whose jobs change because of AI should adapt

items.stem: Using AI to monitor people in public places is unacceptable even if it reduces crime.
items.short: AI monitoring of public places is unacceptable even if it reduces crime
items.source: Handoff A15; Zhang and Dafoe privacy top-tier (N1)

items.stem: Limited AI monitoring is justified when it prevents serious harm.
items.short: limited AI monitoring is justified to prevent serious harm

items.stem: People should be told, and able to object, whenever AI is used to make a decision about them.
items.short: people should be told, and able to object, when AI decides about them

items.stem: The most capable AI models should be released openly so that anyone can study and build on them.
items.short: the most capable AI models should be released openly

items.stem: Some AI models are powerful enough that access should be restricted, even if that makes independent research harder.
items.short: some AI models should have restricted access

items.stem: It is more dangerous for a few companies to control the best AI than for those models to be freely available.
items.short: a few companies controlling the best AI is more dangerous than open release

items.stem: An AI companion can be a real source of comfort without replacing human relationships.
items.short: an AI companion can comfort without replacing human relationships

items.stem: Some parts of life, such as caring for children or for the dying, should stay human-led no matter how capable AI becomes.
items.short: some parts of life should always stay human-led

items.stem: I would welcome AI that helps me think and remember better, even if I came to depend on it.
items.short: you'd welcome AI that helps you think and remember, even if you depended on it

items.stem: Within my lifetime, AI could become capable enough that humans lose the ability to control it.
items.short: AI could become impossible for humans to control within your lifetime

items.stem: Governments should treat the most extreme possible risks from future AI as a top priority, even if that is expensive.
items.short: the most extreme possible risks from future AI should be a top government priority

items.stem: Talk of AI ending humanity distracts from the real harms AI is causing today.
items.short: talk of AI ending humanity distracts from today's harms

items.stem: How often do you use AI tools yourself, such as chatbots, image tools or AI assistants?
items.source: Pew 2026 49% ever use (R8b); Abacus use drives trust (N8)

items.stem: How well do you feel you understand what today's AI can and cannot do?
How settled are your views on the questions you just answered?
options: Not something I have thought about

items.stem: How much do you trust each of these to act in the public interest on AI?
items.source: Zhang and Dafoe (N1); Pew REGCONF (R8); Research Co. (N8)

items.stem: How worried are you that each of these will misuse AI?
Has AI already saved you time, money or effort in a way that mattered to you?
Have you personally been harmed by someone else's use of AI, for example a wrong automated decision, a scam, or lost work?
How important is the future of AI compared with other issues facing your country?
items.source: Handoff A29; AI Impacts <1% top issue (N18)

items.stem: In a few words, how would you describe your view of AI?
Does your work or study involve building or deploying AI?
items.source: Zhang and Dafoe CS degree effect (N1)

items.stem: Where do you live?
A new AI tool could speed up cancer research, but independent experts cannot fully check how it reaches its conclusions. What should happen?
options: Use it in supervised trials first.
Hold it back until independent checks are possible.

items.stem: A small number of companies control the most capable AI systems. Which concerns you most?
options: Too much economic and political power in a few hands.
It depends on how accountable those companies are.

items.stem: A company could do the work of 30 people with 5 by using AI. Which comes closest to your view?
options: Allow it; the economy will adjust.
Allow it only if the company funds retraining or income support for the people replaced.
Keep the human jobs even if products cost more.
Allow it only after a required review of the impact on workers.
items.source: Handoff S03 rewritten to balance options

items.stem: Twenty years from now, which role for AI would you prefer?
options: People and AI decide together, with people holding the final say.
AI stays a tool that people direct.
It depends on how things go.

items.stem: Suppose your country is behind others in advanced AI. Which response do you prefer?
options: Focus on using proven AI to improve everyday services.
